reading.reading_name: Guidance for Standard VII: Responsibilities as a CFA Institute Member or CFA Candidate

drills.los_text: demonstrate a thorough knowledge of the CFA Institute Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct by interpreting the Code and Standards in various situations involving issues of professional integrity
drills.reading_name: Guidance for Standard VII: Responsibilities as a CFA Institute Member or CFA Candidate

questions.stem: Nero, a Level II CFA candidate, finds what appears to be a copy of the Level II exam. Unsure whether it is authentic, he posts some of the questions in an online chatroom, and two other Level II candidates ask him for more and use them to prepare. Under Standard VII(A), a violation has most likely been committed by:

options.A: all three candidates.
options.B: none of the candidates.
options.C: the two recipients only.

rationales.A: Nero and the two candidates violated Standard VII(A). By giving information about the exam questions to two candidates, Nero provided them an unfair advantage and undermined the integrity and validity of the Level II exam as an accurate measure of the knowledge, skills, and abilities necessary to earn the right to use the CFA designation. By soliciting and accepting the information, the two other candidates also compromised the integrity and validity of the exam and undermined the ethical framework that is a key part of the designation.
rationales.B: This reflects the belief that unverified material is exempt. Circulating, soliciting and using suspected exam content still compromises the integrity and validity of the exam; whether the copy was genuine was unknown to all three, and the unfair advantage conferred on candidates who had not yet sat the exam does not wait on that question being settled.
rationales.C: This reflects the recipient-only misconception. The two candidates who solicited and accepted the questions did violate the standard, but so did Nero: as the provider of the exam content he gave them an unfair advantage and undermined the exam as a measure of what a candidate knows.

questions.stem: Chiu registers for the Level I CFA exam and files a free Emergency Deferral request claiming that her uncle has died. After CFA Institute denies it, she files a second request claiming that her mother has died, supported by an altered death certificate. She later admits that no one had died and that she altered the documentation to save money. Her conduct is most likely:

options.A: a violation of Standards VII(A) and I(C).
options.B: not a violation of any standard.
options.C: a violation of Standard I(D) only.

rationales.A: By filing a fraudulent request for an Emergency Deferral, Chiu violated rules of the CFA Program and compromised the integrity of the CFA exam. As a result, her conduct violated Standard VII(A), in addition to Standard I(C) Misrepresentation — the false claims of a death in the family and the altered death certificate were misrepresentations made to CFA Institute in order to obtain a benefit she was not entitled to.
rationales.B: Deferral administration is part of the CFA Program, not a matter outside professional conduct. Fraudulent representations made to CFA Institute about its own programs violate Standard VII(A) directly, because they compromise the rules under which the program is administered, and the falsified documentation separately engages Standard I(C) Misrepresentation.
rationales.C: Conduct involving dishonesty and deceit does raise misconduct concerns, but lying to CFA Institute about program administration compromises the integrity of the CFA Program itself, which is a violation of Standard VII(A). The misrepresentation engaged by the false claims and the altered certificate is Standard I(C), so confining the answer to Standard I(D) misses both standards actually breached.

questions.stem: At a CFA exam test center, Hermosa refuses to cooperate when asked to show that his trouser pockets are empty. He becomes agitated, shouts profanity, throws his passport at the proctor and threatens her, and other candidates complain about the interruption and about their safety. His conduct is most likely:

options.A: a breach of local law but not of the Code and Standards.
options.B: not a violation of any standard.
options.C: a violation of Standard VII(A).

rationales.A: Conduct at a test center falls squarely within Standard VII(A), which reaches any conduct that compromises the reputation or integrity of CFA Institute or the CFA designation, or the validity, integrity and security of its examinations. Whether or not local law is also engaged by the threats, refusing the security check and disrupting the center breach the testing rules and so breach the standard.
rationales.B: Refusing the required security procedure, abusing the proctor and disrupting the other candidates violates the testing rules and compromises the integrity and security of the exam. Rights of expression are not implicated: the testing rules are conditions a candidate accepts in order to sit the exam, and disruptive conduct in the room degrades the exam for everyone present.
rationales.C: Hermosa's conduct violated Standard VII(A) because he violated testing rules and compromised the integrity and security of the CFA exam. Refusing to show that his pockets were empty defeated the security procedure the center is required to apply to every candidate, and the profanity, the thrown passport and the threat to the proctor interrupted the other candidates and called their safety into question.

questions.stem: Yu, a CFA candidate, has difficulty remembering formulas, so she writes several of them on a piece of paper and hides it in her shirt sleeve before entering the computer-based testing room. A proctor sees her removing the paper. Her conduct is most likely:

options.A: not a violation of any standard.
options.B: a violation of Standard VII(A).
options.C: a violation of Standard I(C).

rationales.A: Bringing written material into the exam room violates the testing rules whether or not the candidate consults it. The breach is complete once the information is in the room, because from that point neither the security of the exam nor the validity of the candidate's performance can be assured, and a proctor cannot be asked to establish what a concealed note was used for.
rationales.B: Because Yu took written information into the computer-based testing room, her conduct violated the testing rules and compromised the security and integrity of the CFA exam and the validity of her exam performance. She therefore violated Standard VII(A), which prohibits conduct that compromises the validity, integrity and security of CFA Institute programs.
rationales.C: Breaches of exam security are Standard VII(A) territory. Standard I(C) Misrepresentation concerns untrue statements or omissions made to clients, prospective clients, employers or the public about investment services, qualifications or performance; Yu made no representation to anyone, so that standard is not the one engaged.

questions.stem: Sharma is taking the Level II CFA exam at a computer-based testing center whose rules prohibit looking at other candidates' screens. Wondering whether his exam is the same as his neighbor's, he looks at the neighbor's screen several times; a proctor observes him and the conduct is captured on video. His conduct is most likely:

options.A: a violation of Standard I(D) only.
options.B: a violation of Standard VII(A).
options.C: not a violation of any standard.

rationales.A: Violations of the rules of the exam room compromise the integrity of the CFA Program, so Standard VII(A) is the operative standard. Standard I(D) Misconduct reaches professional conduct involving dishonesty, fraud or deceit, or any act that reflects adversely on professional reputation, competence or integrity generally; the specific prohibition Sharma broke was a testing rule governing his conduct as a candidate.
rationales.B: Sharma's conduct violated Standard VII(A) because he violated testing rules and compromised the validity, integrity, and security of the CFA exam. The prohibition on viewing another candidate's screen exists to keep each candidate's performance his own, and breaching it in full view of a proctor and the center's cameras undermines the exam as an accurate measure of what he knows.
rationales.C: Looking at another candidate's screen breaches the testing rules whatever the motive. Standard VII(A) turns on the conduct and its effect on the validity, integrity and security of the exam, not on whether the candidate set out to copy an answer, and curiosity about whether the neighbor had the same questions is no defense.

questions.stem: After completing the Level II CFA exam, Rossi posts online that she thinks she did especially well on the derivatives questions, that she counted about 18 of them, that the ethics questions were very hard, and that she was surprised there were no questions at all about IPO allocations. Under Standard VII(A), Rossi is most likely:

options.A: not in violation for her difficulty and performance remarks.
options.B: in violation only for her remarks on her own performance.
options.C: not in violation for any of the remarks in her post.

rationales.A: Rossi did not violate Standard VII(A) when she wrote about how difficult she found the exam or how well she thinks she may have done. By revealing portions of the exam content covered and the areas not covered, however, she did violate Standard VII(A). Depending on the time frame in which the comments were posted, she may not only have assisted future candidates but also have provided an unfair advantage to candidates yet to sit for the same exam, thereby undermining the integrity and validity of the exam.
rationales.B: This reverses the rule. Impressions of the exam's difficulty and of one's own performance are permitted; it is the disclosure of which topics were tested, how heavily, and which were absent altogether that breaches the standard, because that is the confidential content of the exam and it is what would advantage a candidate yet to sit it.
rationales.C: This overextends the allowance for opinions. Her remarks on difficulty and on her own performance are permissible, but her account of the content covered and of the areas not covered discloses confidential exam material and violates Standard VII(A), so the post is not blameless in every respect.

questions.stem: A week after completing the Level I CFA exam, Gagne joins a forum discussion thread about the exam's most challenging questions and works with the other posters to determine the correct answers. His conduct is most likely:

options.A: a breach of exam confidentiality.
options.B: a discussion permitted once the exam has been held.
options.C: a permissible aid to future candidates.

rationales.A: Gagne violated Standard VII(A) by providing confidential exam information, which compromises the integrity of the exam process. In trying to determine correct answers to specific questions, the group's discussion included question-specific details that are considered confidential, and contributing to it put that material into circulation regardless of whether he was the first to raise any particular question.
rationales.B: Confidentiality of exam content does not expire when the candidate leaves the test center. Question-specific detail compromises the integrity of the exam process whenever it is disclosed, and a week after one administration there may well be candidates yet to sit the same exam who would be advantaged by it.
rationales.C: Helping future candidates with confidential exam content is the harm the standard guards against, not a justification. An unfair advantage given to candidates who have not yet sat the exam undermines its validity as a measure of each candidate's own knowledge, skills and abilities.

questions.stem: CFA4Sure, a commercial exam preparation service, emails its customers after the exam asking them to share the questions they found hardest so that it can better prepare future customers. Pena, a candidate, replies with a summary of the questions she found most difficult. Under Standard VII(A), a violation has most likely been committed by:

options.A: Neither Pena nor CFA4Sure.
options.B: Pena, the candidate.
options.C: CFA4Sure, not Pena.

rationales.A: Pena replied privately, and to a request she did not initiate, but neither fact changes the analysis. The questions she described are confidential until CFA Institute elects to release them publicly, so disclosing them in a private email breaches Standard VII(A) exactly as a public posting would. The misconception is that a request from someone else supplies permission to disclose; it does not.
rationales.B: Pena violated Standard VII(A) by disclosing exam questions. The information she provided is considered confidential until publicly released by CFA Institute. CFA4Sure is likely to use such feedback to refine its review materials for future candidates, so Pena's sharing of the specific questions undermined the integrity of the exam while potentially making the exam easier for future candidates. If the CFA4Sure employees who participated in soliciting the confidential CFA Program information are themselves CFA Institute members or candidates, they also violated Standard VII(A).
rationales.C: The fault does not shift to the party that asked. Pena is the one who disclosed confidential exam content, so she violated Standard VII(A) herself, and describing the request as a legitimate survey creates no exception. The CFA4Sure employees who solicited the information also violated the standard if they are members or candidates, but that is in addition to Pena's violation, not instead of it.

questions.stem: As a condition of grading CFA exam papers, Whitcomb agrees not to discuss exam materials with anyone other than CFA Institute staff or other graders. Several weeks after grading ends, he tells colleagues who are candidates which question he graded, what the guideline answer was, and that few candidates scored well. Whitcomb's disclosure is most likely:

options.A: prohibited by Standard VII(A).
options.B: permitted after grading.
options.C: permitted grader commentary.

rationales.A: Whitcomb violated Standard VII(A) by disclosing information related to a specific question on the exam, which compromised the integrity of the exam process. He identified the question he graded, gave its guideline answer, and revealed how candidates had performed on it, and he did so to colleagues who are themselves candidates, precisely the audience the confidentiality condition of his grading assignment was meant to exclude.
rationales.B: The confidentiality he accepted as a condition of grading, and the duty under Standard VII(A) itself, survive the end of the engagement. All aspects of an exam remain confidential until CFA Institute elects to release them publicly, so the passage of a few weeks neither releases the question nor authorizes him to discuss it.
rationales.C: Graders hold no commentary privilege. Access to the exam materials was granted on the express condition that he not discuss them except with CFA Institute staff or other graders, and Standard VII(A) prohibits volunteers from offering, soliciting or disclosing confidential material gained while volunteering to unauthorized personnel or those outside the organization. The colleagues he told are candidates, not authorized recipients.

questions.stem: Ramirez works as an investor relations consultant for small companies seeking greater exposure and also serves as program chair for his local CFA Institute society, where he schedules only his own clients to present to the membership. Ramirez most likely violated:

options.A: Standard VII(A).
options.B: Standard VI(C).
options.C: No standard.

rationales.A: By using his volunteer position at CFA Institute to benefit himself and his clients, Ramirez is compromising the reputation and integrity of CFA Institute and thus is violating Standard VII(A). Improperly using an association with CFA Institute to achieve personal or professional goals is expressly among the conduct the standard prohibits, and scheduling only his own clients to present turns a volunteer role into a marketing channel for his consulting practice.
rationales.B: Standard VI(C) governs referral fees, and no referral fee or other payment from the presenting companies is described. The defect is not an undisclosed payment but the misuse of the CFA Institute association: Ramirez steers a society benefit to his own client list, which is addressed by Standard VII(A).
rationales.C: Program chair is a volunteer position, but volunteering for CFA Institute brings a member inside the Code and Standards rather than outside them. Using the discretion the role carries to advance one's own clients compromises the reputation and integrity of CFA Institute, which is what Standard VII(A) reaches.

questions.stem: Warrenski serves on the CFA Institute GIPS Standards Technical Committee, which gives her advance knowledge of confidential information about coming changes to the GIPS standards, and she tells clients that her committee membership will allow her to assist them better in keeping up with those changes. Warrenski's conduct is best described as:

options.A: no more than a factual statement of her role.
options.B: a violation of Standard VII(A).
options.C: a permitted client benefit.

rationales.A: Warrenski may factually state her involvement with the committee, and that much would be unobjectionable. What she did goes further: she presented the position as a strategic business advantage over competing firms and implied that confidential committee information would be used for her clients' benefit, which is promotion rather than factual description.
rationales.B: Warrenski used her association with the GIPS Standards Technical Committee to promote her firm's services to clients and potential clients. In stating that her volunteer position at CFA Institute provides a strategic business advantage over competing firms, and in implying to clients that she would use confidential information to further their interests, she compromised the reputation and integrity of CFA Institute and thus violated Standard VII(A). She may factually state her involvement with the committee, but she cannot infer any special advantage to her clients from that participation.
rationales.C: A benefit to clients is not a defense. Her advance knowledge is confidential material gained through participation in a CFA Institute program, and Standard VII(A) bars leveraging it for competitive advantage however much a client might gain. The conduct that attracts the clients is the same conduct that compromises the Institute's reputation and integrity.

questions.stem: Park, a Level II candidate frustrated with her exam preparation provider, posts on a third-party discussion board, "How could your service provide such limited instructional resources on the analysis of inventories and taxes when the exam had multiple questions about them?" Park most likely violated the Code and Standards by:

options.A: revealing topics tested on the exam.
options.B: purchasing third-party review material.
options.C: offering her opinion on the exam's difficulty.

rationales.A: Park violated the Code and Standards by providing specific information on topics tested on the exam. Standard VII(A) prohibits providing information to candidates or the public that is considered confidential to the CFA Program, and in revealing that questions related to the analysis of inventories and the analysis of taxes were on the exam, she disclosed broad topical areas tested, which remain confidential until CFA Institute elects to release them. Posting on a third-party board rather than writing privately widens the audience but is not what creates the violation.
rationales.B: Candidates are not prohibited from using outside resources. Buying or studying from third-party review material is permitted, and the violation lies in what Park wrote about the exam rather than in where she had prepared.
rationales.C: The guidance for the standard explicitly acknowledges that members and candidates are allowed to offer their opinions about the CFA Program. Park could have complained about thin coverage of inventories and taxes without identifying them as subject matter that appeared on the exam; it is the disclosure of what was tested, not the complaint, that breaches Standard VII(A).

questions.stem: Under Standard VII(A), the confidentiality owed to CFA Institute exam material is best described as covering:

options.A: the verbatim text of exam questions.
options.B: all exam content apart from sharing with later-window candidates.
options.C: all confidential material from any program or exam process.

rationales.A: The prohibition reaches well beyond verbatim text. Examples of information that cannot be disclosed by candidates or members include specific details of questions appearing on an exam and broad topical areas and formulas tested or not tested on an exam, so describing an exam's format or topic emphasis is itself a disclosure of confidential material.
rationales.B: Sharing with candidates who sit a later window of the same cycle is among the most direct compromises of exam integrity, because it hands them information about material still in use. All aspects of an exam for any CFA Institute program are confidential until CFA Institute elects to release them publicly, and nothing in the standard opens a window inside a cycle.
rationales.C: Participants in CFA Institute programs are prohibited from disclosing confidential material gained during participation in any program or any exam process. Examples of information that cannot be disclosed by candidates or members include, but are not limited to, (1) specific details of questions appearing on an exam and (2) broad topical areas and formulas tested or not tested on an exam. All aspects of an exam for any CFA Institute program are considered confidential until such time as CFA Institute elects to release them publicly.

questions.stem: Under Standard VII(A), the conduct the standard prohibits is best described as:

options.A: an exhaustive list of violations.
options.B: cheating on the examination.
options.C: a nonexhaustive list including cheating.

rationales.A: The guidance is framed as conduct that includes but is not limited to the items listed, so conduct that appears nowhere on the list can still violate the standard. Reading the enumeration as closed would invite precisely the behavior the standard exists to catch.
rationales.B: Cheating is one item on a longer list. Prohibited conduct also covers violating the rules, regulations, and testing policies of CFA Institute programs; providing confidential program or exam information to candidates or the public; disregarding or attempting to circumvent security measures established for any CFA Institute examinations; improperly using an association with CFA Institute to achieve personal or professional goals; and misrepresenting information to CFA Institute regarding any CFA Institute program.
rationales.C: Prohibited conduct includes but is not limited to giving or receiving assistance (cheating) on any CFA Institute examinations; violating the rules, regulations, and testing policies of CFA Institute programs; providing confidential program or exam information to candidates or the public; disregarding or attempting to circumvent security measures established for any CFA Institute examinations; improperly using an association with CFA Institute to achieve personal or professional goals; and misrepresenting information to CFA Institute regarding any CFA Institute program. Because the enumeration is open, conduct it does not name can still violate the standard.

questions.stem: Under Standard VII(A), a member's expression of a personal opinion about CFA Institute or its programs is most likely:

options.A: prohibited by the standard.
options.B: not covered by the standard.
options.C: subject to CFA Institute approval.

rationales.A: Standard VII(A) does not reach opinions at all. Members and candidates may disagree with CFA Institute and say so, and treating criticism as a violation confuses confidential exam content, which is protected, with views about the organization and its policies, which are not.
rationales.B: Standard VII(A) does not cover expressing opinions regarding CFA Institute or its programs. Members and candidates are free to disagree and express their disagreement with CFA Institute on its policies, its procedures, or any advocacy positions taken by the organization. When expressing a personal opinion, a candidate is still prohibited from disclosing confidential information about exam content, including any actual exam questions and information about subject matter covered or not covered in an exam.
rationales.C: No pre-approval regime exists. Members and candidates may voice disagreement with the Institute's policies, procedures and advocacy positions without any clearance, and the only limit on a personal opinion is that it must not carry confidential exam content.

questions.stem: Under Standard VII(A), a candidate's discussion of nonconfidential material in a study group is most likely:

options.A: a violation of the standard.
options.B: permissible preparation for an exam.
options.C: a registered group's privilege.

rationales.A: Collaborative study is ordinary preparation, not a breach. No unfair advantage arises from material that is not confidential in the first place, and what the standard polices is the content a group trades in rather than the fact that candidates prepare together.
rationales.B: Standard VII(A) does not prohibit candidates from discussing nonconfidential information or material with others or in study groups in preparation for an exam. What a study group may not trade in is confidential CFA Program material: actual exam questions, specific details of questions appearing on an exam, and broad topical areas and formulas tested or not tested on an exam.
rationales.C: No registration or supervision regime for study groups exists. The boundary the standard draws is the confidentiality of the material discussed, not the format in which candidates choose to prepare.

questions.stem: Under Standard VII(A), a member who volunteers in a CFA Institute program is most likely:

options.A: free to share deliberations after the assignment.
options.B: often exposed to confidential material.
options.C: exempt from confidentiality when unpaid.

rationales.A: Confidentiality does not lapse when the assignment does. Deliberation related to an exam process is among the material a volunteer must not share, and it stays confidential until CFA Institute elects to release it, so disclosure after the engagement ends still violates Standard VII(A).
rationales.B: Members participating as volunteers in CFA Institute programs are often exposed to confidential material. That exposure is why Standard VII(A) prohibits members from offering, soliciting or disclosing confidential material gained while volunteering to unauthorized personnel or those outside the organization. Examples of information that must not be shared by members involved in developing, administering, or grading exams include but are not limited to: (1) questions appearing on an exam or under consideration; (2) deliberation related to an exam process; and (3) information related to the scoring of questions.
rationales.C: Serving without compensation confers no exemption. Volunteers are members, and the access their service gives them to questions under consideration, exam deliberations and scoring information is the reason Standard VII(A) binds them.

questions.stem: Standard VII(A) most likely requires compliance with the Code and Standards from:

options.A: members and candidates involved with an Institute program.
options.B: every program participant, whether a member or not.
options.C: participants, but only while the examination is under way.

rationales.A: Standard VII(A) holds members and candidates to high ethical conduct while they are participating in or involved with any CFA Institute program, so as not to undermine the public's confidence in the integrity of those programs. The standard does not require a participant in a CFA Institute program to comply with the Code and Standards unless that person is a member or candidate who is otherwise subject to them. The duty therefore attaches to the person's status as a member or candidate, and it runs across the whole of that person's involvement with a program rather than only while an examination is in progress.
rationales.B: The standard reaches members and candidates, not every participant. A participant who is neither a member nor a candidate is not brought under the full Code and Standards by Standard VII(A), because the standard imposes no such obligation on non-members; binding every participant to the entire Code overstates its scope.
rationales.C: The duty is not confined to examination hours. Standard VII(A) covers participating in, or being involved with, any CFA Institute program, which includes grading, volunteering, item writing and other program activity, so conduct away from the testing room is equally within its reach.

questions.stem: With respect to candidates' use of online services in preparing for the examinations, the practice of CFA Institute is best described as:

options.A: policing blogs and forums for confidential information.
options.B: taking violation reports only from staff and volunteers.
options.C: leaving third-party blogs and social media unmonitored.

rationales.A: Many candidates for the CFA designation use online services as part of their exam preparations. CFA Institute actively polices blogs, forums and related social networking groups for dissemination of confidential information. The organization works to promptly address or remove any and all material that violates exam or other rules, laws or regulations, and candidates, members and the public are encouraged to report suspected violations to CFA Institute.
rationales.B: Reporting is not restricted to insiders. Candidates, members and the public are all encouraged to report suspected violations to CFA Institute, so limiting the reporting channel to the organization's own staff and volunteers misstates the guidance.
rationales.C: The guidance states the opposite. CFA Institute actively polices blogs, forums and related social networking groups for the dissemination of confidential information, and works to promptly address or remove any material that violates exam or other rules, laws or regulations.

questions.stem: Under Standard VII(A), the rules, regulations and policies for CFA Institute programs are best described as:

options.A: defining allowed and disallowed actions beyond the Code.
options.B: defining a breach only when a scoring advantage results.
options.C: defining a breach only as the admission ticket shows it.

rationales.A: The rules, regulations and policies for CFA Institute programs define additional allowed and disallowed actions concerning the programs and examinations. Violating any of the testing policies constitutes a violation of Standard VII(A). The policies for CFA Institute programs are posted on the CFA Institute website, where participants are expected to find and read them.
rationales.B: Advantage is not an element of the violation. Violating any of the testing policies is itself a breach of Standard VII(A), whether or not the candidate gained anything in scoring terms from the breach; the standard asks whether a policy was broken, not whether it paid off.
rationales.C: The published rules, regulations and policies of the programs govern, and they are posted on the CFA Institute website rather than confined to what appears on an admission ticket. A breach of any of them is a violation of Standard VII(A).

questions.stem: Zonder's firm, AZ, advertises that all of its principals are CFA charterholders who passed the three examinations on the first attempt, and the advertisement prominently links this to the superior performance of the firm's mutual funds. Under Standard VII(B), the advertisement is most likely:

options.A: improper, as it cites the principals' charterholder status.
options.B: improper, as it ties first-attempt passes to performance.
options.C: proper, as each statement it makes is factually accurate.

rationales.A: A truthful reference to the principals' charters is permitted, and communicating that a professional has earned the designation is encouraged rather than restricted. The defect in this advertisement is the linkage drawn between exam results and investment performance, not the mention of the credential itself.
rationales.B: Zonder may state that all AZ principals passed the three examinations on the first try as long as this statement is true, but it must not be linked to performance or imply superior ability. Implying that (1) CFA charterholders achieve better investment results and (2) those who pass the exams on the first try may be more successful than those who do not violates Standard VII(B).
rationales.C: Every statement in an advertisement can be true and the advertisement still improper. The first-attempt statement becomes a violation once it is linked to the funds' performance, because the juxtaposition creates the misleading implication that charterholders, and first-time passers in particular, obtain superior investment results.

questions.stem: Five years after receiving his CFA charter, Vasseur resigns and travels abroad for two years, filing no Professional Conduct Statement and paying no dues, and his membership lapses. Without reinstating it, he becomes a self-employed analyst and prints business cards displaying 'CFA' after his name. His use of the designation is most likely:

options.A: improper, as his lapsed membership ended that right.
options.B: proper, as dues obligations pause during residence abroad.
options.C: proper, as a charter once earned is held permanently.

rationales.A: Vasseur violated Standard VII(B) by misrepresenting his status as a charterholder, because he is no longer a CFA Institute member with the right to use the CFA designation. He therefore is no longer able to state or imply that he is a CFA charterholder. If he wants to reinstate his membership, he needs to complete the appropriate process and meet the requirements for reinstatement established by CFA Institute.
rationales.B: Nothing tolls the membership requirements for time spent abroad. The Professional Conduct Statement and the annual dues remain due; once they go unmet the membership lapses, and present-tense use of the designation is a misrepresentation wherever the former member happens to be living.
rationales.C: Passing the examinations and earning the charter is not by itself a permanent entitlement to use the designation. The right to use it depends on maintaining the requirements for membership, which include filing the Professional Conduct Statement and paying dues, so a lapse removes the right until the member completes the reinstatement process.

questions.stem: After a 25-year career Simpson retires, files no Professional Conduct Statement and pays no dues, and designs a plain business card that continues to put 'CFA' after his name. His continued use of the designation is most likely:

options.A: improper, as his lapsed membership ended that right.
options.B: proper, as a plain card makes no promotional claim.
options.C: proper, as retirement preserves the designation.

rationales.A: By misrepresenting his status as a charterholder, Simpson violated Standard VII(B). Because he failed to meet the requirements for membership established by CFA Institute, his membership lapsed and he has given up the right to use the CFA designation. CFA Institute has procedures, however, for reclassifying a member and charterholder as retired and reducing the annual dues; if he wants to obtain retired status, he needs to complete the appropriate process and meet the requirements for retired status established by CFA Institute.
rationales.B: A modest, non-promotional format does not cure the misrepresentation. Standard VII(B) is breached by any present-tense use of the designation once membership has lapsed, whatever the design of the card or letterhead on which it appears.
rationales.C: Retirement is not automatic and does not of itself preserve the designation. CFA Institute has a process for reclassifying a member and charterholder as retired at reduced annual dues, but until Simpson completes that process and meets its requirements, his lapsed membership forfeits the right to use the designation.

questions.stem: In conversation with a friend who is considering candidacy, Reese says she learned a great deal as a CFA candidate, notes that many firms require their employees to be CFA charterholders, and recommends the CFA Program to anyone pursuing a career in investment management. Her comments are most likely:

options.A: proper, as nothing she says misrepresents the CFA.
options.B: improper, as she recommends the program to others.
options.C: improper, as she cites firms' hiring requirements.

rationales.A: Reese's comments comply with Standard VII(B). Her statements refer to facts: earning her CFA designation enhanced her knowledge, and many firms require the CFA designation for their investment professionals. Factual, verifiable statements about what the program taught her and about industry hiring practice are permitted, and recommending the program to someone pursuing a career in investment management misrepresents nothing about the meaning or implications of candidacy or the designation.
rationales.B: Recommending the CFA Program is permitted. Standard VII(B) bars misrepresentation of the meaning or implications of membership, candidacy or the designation; it does not prohibit encouraging someone to become a candidate, and Reese promises nothing about what candidacy will deliver.
rationales.C: That many firms require the designation of their investment professionals is a factual statement about industry practice, and Standard VII(B) expressly permits it. It neither exaggerates what the designation means nor links the credential to investment performance.

questions.stem: Glass, the lead quantitative analyst at a hedge fund, wants to comment anonymously on an article on an investor blog using information drawn from his work, and publishes the comment over the signature line 'Expert, CFA'. His comment is most likely:

options.A: improper only under Standard IV(A), for using work information.
options.B: improper under Standard VII(B), for the pseudonymous claim.
options.C: proper, as he does in fact hold the CFA charter.

rationales.A: Drawing on information from his employer raises a separate loyalty question under Standard IV(A), and that concern may well exist, but it is not the only failing here. Signing the comment 'Expert, CFA' is itself an improper use of the designation under Standard VII(B), and that is the violation the item turns on.
rationales.B: Using a fictitious name or pseudonym to hide one's true identity while still claiming to be a charterholder is a misrepresentation and an improper use of the designation. By using 'Expert, CFA,' Glass violated Standard VII(B).
rationales.C: Holding the charter does not cure the concealment. Claiming the designation from behind a fictitious identity is an improper use of it, because the reader cannot connect the credential to the person asserting it; the accuracy of the credential is beside the point.

questions.stem: Albert's business card reads 'Judy Albert, CFA Level II'. Tye's promotional material describes the requirements of the CFA Program and indicates that he participates in the program and has completed Levels I and II. Under Standard VII(B), a violation has most likely been committed by:

options.A: Tye only.
options.B: Albert and Tye.
options.C: Albert only.

rationales.A: The problem lies with Albert's card, not with Tye's material. Tye merely indicates in promotional material that he is participating in the CFA Program and has completed Levels I and II, which candidates are permitted to communicate, so he is the one who has not violated the standard.
rationales.B: Only Albert violated. The reference on Albert's business card implies that there is a 'CFA Level II' designation, and candidates may not imply that some sort of partial designation is earned by passing a level of the exam. Tye's statement that he participates in the CFA Program and has completed Levels I and II is a permitted factual communication, so he did not violate Standard VII(B).
rationales.C: Albert violated the Standards, but Tye did not. The reference on Albert's business card implies that there is a 'CFA Level II' designation; candidates may not imply that there is some sort of partial designation earned after passing a level of the CFA exam, so Albert violated Standard VII(B). Tye merely indicates in promotional material that he is participating in the CFA Program and has completed Levels I and II, and candidates may communicate that they are participating in the CFA Program and may state the levels they have completed, so Tye has not violated Standard VII(B).

questions.stem: Rule, who recently earned the CFA charter, states in marketing material: 'While completing the examination process in three consecutive years, I consistently received the highest possible scores on the topics of ethics, alternative investments, and portfolio management.' Under Standard VII(B), the material is most likely:

options.A: proper in every respect.
options.B: improper as to the consecutive-year claim.
options.C: improper as to the highest-score claim.

rationales.A: The material is not wholly proper, because the score claim violates Standard VII(B). CFA Program candidates do not receive their actual scores on the exam, so Rule cannot factually state that he received the highest possible scores in any topic area.
rationales.B: Stating that the examinations were completed in three consecutive years is not a violation as long as it is true. Standard VII(B) does not prohibit the communication of factual information about completing the CFA Program in three consecutive years, so this part of the material is permitted.
rationales.C: Rule violated Standard VII(B) in stating that he received the highest scores on the topics of ethics, alternative investments, and portfolio management. CFA Program candidates do not receive their actual scores on the exam: topic and subtopic results are grouped into three broad categories, and the exam is graded only as pass or fail. Although candidates may achieve a topical score of above 70%, they cannot factually state that they received the highest possible score, because that information is not reported. Stating that the exams were completed in three consecutive years, by contrast, is not a violation as long as it is true.

questions.stem: Under Standard VII(B), the individuals covered by the term 'CFA Institute member' are most likely:

options.A: Regular members only, with affiliate members excluded.
options.B: Regular and affiliate members in good standing.
options.C: Anyone who has ever passed a CFA examination.

rationales.A: Both regular and affiliate members fall within the definition. Standard VII(B) draws no line that puts affiliate members outside the term, so an answer restricting it to regular members understates the population the standard covers.
rationales.B: The term 'CFA Institute member' refers to regular and affiliate members of CFA Institute who have met the membership requirements as defined in the CFA Institute Bylaws. Those requirements must be satisfied on an annual basis: complete a CFA Institute Membership Agreement; remit to CFA Institute a completed Professional Conduct Statement, which renews the commitment to abide by the requirements of the Code and Standards and the CFA Institute Professional Conduct Program; and pay applicable CFA Institute membership dues. Membership therefore turns on meeting, and continuing to meet, those annual conditions rather than on the category of member alone.
rationales.C: Membership requires meeting the Institute's defined membership requirements, not merely passing an examination. Passing one level, or all three, confers no membership: the individual must complete the Membership Agreement, file the Professional Conduct Statement and pay applicable dues each year.

questions.stem: Under Standard VII(B), a member who fails to meet a membership requirement most likely:

options.A: Remains a member in dues arrears.
options.B: Keeps full designation use during a grace period.
options.C: Is no longer considered a CFA Institute member.

rationales.A: The consequence is loss of membership status, not a billing footnote. An unmet requirement does not leave the individual a member whose account is simply overdue; the individual ceases to be a member until membership is reactivated.
rationales.B: There is no grace period that preserves use of the marks. An individual failing any membership requirement is no longer considered a member, and present-tense references to membership must stop immediately rather than continue for a transition window.
rationales.C: If a CFA Institute member fails to meet any membership requirement established by CFA Institute, the individual is no longer considered a member. Until membership is reactivated, individuals must not present themselves to others as members and must remove all references to CFA Institute membership from social media profiles, business communications, reports, and anywhere else membership is referenced. Former members may state, however, that they were CFA Institute members in the past, or refer to the years when they met the requirements of CFA Institute membership.

questions.stem: Under Standard VII(B), the right to use the CFA designation most likely:

options.A: Vests permanently once granted, with no annual conditions.
options.B: Belongs to the firm employing the charterholder.
options.C: Belongs to the individual who earned it, maintained annually.

rationales.A: The right to use the designation is maintained through the Institute's annual membership requirements; it does not vest permanently at the moment the charter is awarded. A charterholder who stops satisfying those requirements forfeits the right to use the designation.
rationales.B: The designation is personal to the individual who earned it and is never an asset of the employing firm. A firm cannot hold, assign, or retain a charterholder's right to use the marks, and it does not lose or gain that right when the charterholder changes employer.
rationales.C: CFA charterholders are those individuals who have earned the right to use the CFA designation granted by CFA Institute. Charterholders are encouraged to use the designation but, in doing so, must state their charterholder status in a manner that is accurate and does not exaggerate the benefits of the charter; use of the designation may be accompanied by an accurate explanation of the requirements that have been met to earn the right to use it. Once granted the right to use the designation, individuals must also satisfy CFA Institute annual membership requirements to maintain that right, and a charterholder who fails to meet any membership requirement forfeits the right to use the CFA designation.

questions.stem: Under Standard VII(B), the conditions establishing candidacy for the CFA designation are most likely:

options.A: An initial registration plus indefinite continuation thereafter.
options.B: A curriculum order plus an intent to sit.
options.C: An accepted application plus enrollment or pending results.

rationales.A: Candidacy lapses whenever the person no longer meets the definition, so it does not run indefinitely from a first registration. An individual who declines to sit for an exam for which he or she enrolled is no longer a candidate, and candidacy resumes only once the person is enrolled to sit for a future examination.
rationales.B: Candidacy requires an accepted application together with current enrollment or a result still pending. Buying or ordering curriculum materials confers nothing, however firm the intent to sit, because CFA Institute has issued no notice of acceptance and the person is not enrolled for a specified examination.
rationales.C: A person is a candidate for the CFA designation if CFA Institute has accepted the person's application to be a candidate for the designation, as evidenced by issuance of a notice of acceptance, and the person is enrolled to sit for a specified examination or has sat for a specified examination but exam results have not yet been received. If an individual declines to sit for an exam for which they have enrolled, or otherwise does not meet the definition of a candidate as described in the CFA Institute Bylaws, that individual is no longer considered a candidate; once the person is enrolled to sit for a future examination, his or her candidacy resumes.

questions.stem: Under Standard VII(B), a candidate's reference to a partial designation is most likely:

options.A: Prohibited unless CFA Institute authorizes it.
options.B: Permitted internally but not in client materials.
options.C: Permitted in any truthful form, such as 'CFA Level II.'

rationales.A: Candidates must not state or imply that they have achieved any type of partial designation in a manner not authorized or permitted by CFA Institute. Except and only to the extent authorized or permitted by CFA Institute, candidates for the CFA designation must never state or imply that they have a partial designation as a result of passing one or more levels of the CFA exam. Candidates also must not cite an expected completion date for earning the charter, because final award of the charter is subject to meeting the requirements for the designation established by CFA Institute and approval by the CFA Institute Board of Governors.
rationales.B: No internal-use carve-out exists. The prohibition reaches any representation of a partial designation, whether it appears in client-facing material, an internal firm document, a business card, a resume or a social media profile.
rationales.C: 'CFA Level II' used as a credential implies a partial designation, which is prohibited however truthful the underlying fact. Only formats authorized or permitted by CFA Institute are available, such as stating that one has passed Level II of the CFA Program, which reports the exam result without claiming a designation.

questions.stem: Under Standard VII(B), a candidate who states that she passed each level of the exam in consecutive sittings most likely:

options.A: Does not violate the standard.
options.B: Violates the standard through self-promotion.
options.C: Violates the standard absent written approval.

rationales.A: If a candidate passes each level of the exam in consecutive sittings and states that he or she did so, that is not a violation of Standard VII(B), because it is a statement of fact. If the candidate then goes on to claim or imply superior ability as a result of obtaining the designation and not failing any of the exams, however, he or she is in violation of Standard VII(B). The line therefore falls between reporting what happened and drawing an inference about one's ability from it.
rationales.B: A true factual statement of consecutive passes is permitted and is not self-promotional in itself. The violation arises only where the candidate goes further and claims or implies superior ability from having passed every level without failing one.
rationales.C: No approval regime exists for factual statements about one's own exam history. Standard VII(B) requires that such statements be accurate and that they not imply superior ability; it does not require clearance from CFA Institute before publication.

questions.stem: Under Standard VII(B), statements emphasizing members' commitment to ethical conduct and the rigor of the CFA exams are most likely:

options.A: Appropriate only if supported by documentation.
options.B: Appropriate as stated.
options.C: Inappropriate and best avoided.

rationales.A: Opinions may be expressed as opinions; it is statements of fact that must be supported. The standard treats the two differently rather than demanding documentary support for both, so requiring support for an opinion misstates the test.
rationales.B: Statements that highlight or emphasize the commitment of CFA Institute members, CFA charterholders and CFA candidates to ethical and professional conduct, or that mention the thoroughness and rigor of the CFA exams, are appropriate. Members and candidates may make claims about the relative merits of CFA Institute, the CFA exams, or the Code and Standards as long as those statements are implicitly or explicitly stated as the opinion of the speaker. Statements that do not express opinions must be supported by facts.
rationales.C: Such statements are appropriate when framed properly, so avoiding the subject is unnecessary. The guidance distinguishes fact from opinion rather than banning claims about members' ethical commitment or the rigor of the examinations.

questions.stem: Under Standard VII(B), a charterholder's claim that CFA charterholders achieve better performance results is most likely:

options.A: Proper if framed as the speaker's opinion.
options.B: Improper in any framing.
options.C: Proper if supported by performance data.

rationales.A: This overextends the opinion allowance. Asserting that the designation produces superior investment performance is barred even when phrased as the speaker's opinion; the allowance covers claims about the relative merits of CFA Institute, the exams, and the Code and Standards, not claims about investment results.
rationales.B: The claim that CFA charterholders achieve better performance results is an improper reference, because it ties the CFA designation to superior investment performance, which Standard VII(B) prohibits. The acceptable counterpart speaks to knowledge and skill rather than results: saying that becoming a charterholder has enhanced one's portfolio management skills describes an improvement in the speaker's own capability and makes no claim about performance.
rationales.C: No amount of supporting data cures a claim that ties the designation to superior investment performance. Standard VII(B) prohibits that claim outright, so documented outcomes do not make the statement proper.

questions.stem: Under Standard VII(B), the references 'CFA, Level II' and 'I passed the Level II CFA exam' are most likely:

options.A: proper in both cases.
options.B: improper only in the case of 'I passed the Level II CFA exam.'
options.C: improper only in the case of 'CFA, Level II.'

rationales.A: The two references are not both proper. 'CFA, Level II' used as a credential implies a partial designation, which Standard VII(B) prohibits, so one of the pair fails even though the underlying fact is true.
rationales.B: This reverses the rule. Candidates may state as a matter of fact which levels of the examination they have completed, so naming the level is not itself the problem; the problem is presenting a level as though it were a designation.
rationales.C: 'CFA, Level II' is improper because it implies a partial designation, and candidates must never state or imply that they hold a partial designation as a result of passing one or more levels of the exam. 'I passed the Level II CFA exam' is proper: it is a factual statement about having completed an examination and claims no designation.

questions.stem: Under Standard VII(B), the references 'CFA, Expected 20XX' and 'John Smith, Charter Pending' are most likely:

options.A: improper only in the case of 'Charter Pending.'
options.B: improper in both cases.
options.C: proper in both cases.

rationales.A: Candidates may not cite an expected completion date for earning the charter, so 'CFA, Expected 20XX' is improper on the same footing as 'Charter Pending' rather than permitted alongside it.
rationales.B: Both 'CFA, Expected 20XX' and 'John Smith, Charter Pending' are improper references. An expected completion date and a 'Charter Pending' label each imply progress toward a charter that cannot be guaranteed: final award of the charter is subject to meeting the requirements for the designation established by CFA Institute and approval by the CFA Institute Board of Governors. A proper reference states the facts and the condition that remains outstanding, as in saying that one has passed all three levels of the CFA exam and will be eligible for the CFA charter upon completion of the required work experience.
rationales.C: Expected dates and 'Charter Pending' imply a completion that is not assured, so neither is an accurate description of a candidate's progress; both are improper rather than both proper.

questions.stem: A charterholder's marketing brochure states, "As a CFA charterholder, I am the most qualified to manage client investments." Under Standard VII(B), the statement is most likely:

options.A: acceptable, because the charterholder sincerely believes it is so.
options.B: improper, because it does not state the year the charter was earned.
options.C: improper, because it claims superiority based on the designation.

rationales.A: Sincerity does not support an unsupported claim of superiority tied to the designation. Standard VII(B) prohibits members and candidates from making statements that promise competence or superior performance on the basis of CFA Institute membership, the CFA designation, or candidacy in the CFA Program. The test is whether the claim can be substantiated, not whether the speaker believes it; a genuinely held but unsupportable belief in one's own superiority is exactly what the standard is written to catch.
rationales.B: The defect is the superiority claim itself, not a missing date. Adding the year the charter was earned would leave "the most qualified to manage client investments" standing, and that comparative claim is the violation. Standard VII(B) does not require that references to the designation carry the year it was awarded; it requires that whatever is said about the designation be factual and supportable.
rationales.C: The statement is improper because it makes an unsupported claim of superior qualification based on nothing more than holding the designation. Earning the charter attests to completion of a rigorous program; it does not establish that its holder is better at managing client assets than any other practitioner, and no evidence is offered that would support the comparison. Standard VII(B) permits factual statements about the benefits of earning the designation, so a proper alternative would be: "The credibility that the CFA designation affords and the skills the CFA Program cultivates are key assets for my future career development." That version describes what the designation and the program provide without promising a level of competence or performance relative to others.

questions.stem: A firm's website states, "John Smith is among the elite, having passed all three CFA exams in three consecutive attempts." Under Standard VII(B), the statement is most likely:

options.A: improper, because a candidate's attempt history is confidential.
options.B: improper, because “among the elite” claims unsupported superiority.
options.C: acceptable, because the passing record it reports is factual.

rationales.A: The facts about the exam history are not the problem and are not forbidden. Stating that an individual passed all three CFA exams in three consecutive sittings is a verifiable factual representation and is entirely permissible under Standard VII(B). It is the characterization layered on top of those facts that crosses the line, so treating the attempt history itself as confidential misstates the standard.
rationales.B: Describing the charterholder as "among the elite" inserts an unsupported claim of superiority and links it to the fact of consecutive passing. Standard VII(B) prohibits statements that over-promise competence or imply superior ability by reason of membership, the designation, or candidacy, and passing on consecutive attempts supports no such inference about investment skill. Stripping the superlative leaves a compliant statement: "John Smith passed all three CFA exams in three consecutive sittings." That version conveys the same verifiable information and makes no comparative claim.
rationales.C: True facts do not rescue the framing. The embedded factual claim is accurate, but "among the elite" is a separate assertion, and that assertion implies superior ability derived from the exam record. A statement can be built from true components and still violate Standard VII(B) if the overall impression it creates promises competence or distinction the designation does not confer.

questions.stem: The purpose of Standard VII(B), Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program, is best described as:

options.A: protecting the licensing revenue CFA Institute earns on the marks.
options.B: requiring factual references and barring promises of competence.
options.C: confining the marks to correspondence with CFA Institute.

rationales.A: The standard is aimed at accuracy of representation to the investing public, not at the economics of the marks. Trademark protection is a separate commercial matter handled through CFA Institute's licensing and legal arrangements. Standard VII(B) sits in the Code and Standards because misleading references to membership, the designation, or candidacy mislead clients and prospects about a member's competence, which is a professional conduct question rather than a revenue question.
rationales.B: Standard VII(B) is intended to assure factual representations relating to CFA Institute and to prohibit members and candidates from making unsupported statements promising competence or performance that are tied to CFA Institute membership, the CFA designation, or candidacy in the CFA Program. Its two halves work together: say what is true about the credential, and do not convert the credential into a promise of results. The standard is not intended to prohibit factual statements about the positive benefits of earning the CFA designation, so describing the credibility the designation affords or the skills the program cultivates remains permissible.
rationales.C: Use of the marks is encouraged, not forbidden. Members and candidates may reference the designation on letterhead, business cards, biographies, directory listings, advertising, websites, and resumes, and may describe the benefits of having earned it. What the standard targets is misrepresentation and unsupported claims, ensuring that references are factual; confining the marks to correspondence with CFA Institute would defeat the purpose of a credential meant to be communicated to clients and prospects.

questions.stem: The communications to which Standard VII(B) applies are best described as:

options.A: oral statements as well as written and electronic ones.
options.B: written and electronic communications, but not oral ones.
options.C: every medium apart from social media profiles.

rationales.A: Standard VII(B) applies to any form of communication, including but not limited to communications made in electronic or written form, such as firm letterhead, business cards, professional biographies, directory listings, printed advertising, LinkedIn pages, email signatures, websites, and personal resumes, and including oral statements made to the public, to clients, or to prospects. The breadth is deliberate: the harm the standard addresses is a misleading impression about competence tied to the designation, and that impression can be created as easily in a client meeting as in a brochure. The medium is irrelevant to the analysis; the content of the representation is what matters.
rationales.B: Oral statements are covered by Standard VII(B) alongside written and electronic ones. An unsupported claim of superior ability made verbally to a prospect is a violation of VII(B) in its own right, not merely a misrepresentation question under Standard I(C). Confining the standard to documents would leave the most common setting for casual overstatement entirely unregulated.
rationales.C: Platform constraints do not create an exemption for social media. Profile fields, character limits, and display formatting are outside the member's control, but the obligation to make only factual, supportable references to membership, the designation, or candidacy is not relaxed on that account. Social media profiles are expressly within the forms of communication the standard reaches, and if a platform cannot accommodate an accurate reference, the member's remedy is to omit the reference rather than to make an inaccurate one.

questions.stem: Under Standard VII(B), a member's use of a pseudonym created to hide her identity on social media is most likely:

options.A: prohibited, with or without the designation.
options.B: permitted, and the designation may be attached.
options.C: permitted, but without the CFA designation attached.

rationales.A: Expressing opinions anonymously is not itself a violation. Members and candidates are free to comment under a pseudonym or an online profile name, and nothing in Standard VII(B) requires that every utterance be made under one's own name. The violation arises only from pairing the anonymity with a claim to the designation, so a blanket prohibition on anonymous commentary overstates the requirement.
rationales.B: The truth of the underlying claim does not cure the problem. The member may in fact hold the charter, but tagging a profile built to conceal her identity with the designation detaches the credential from the person accountable for it. A reader cannot verify the claim, and CFA Institute cannot connect the conduct to a member, which is precisely the accountability the standard preserves.
rationales.C: On social media, where individuals may anonymously express their opinions, pseudonyms or online profile names created to hide a member's identity must not be tagged with the CFA designation. The two are permissible separately and impermissible together: anonymous opinion is fine, and an identified profile may carry the designation, but a deliberately concealing identity may not claim the credential. Reference to the designation carries a representation about an identifiable person's qualifications, and that representation cannot be made from behind a name chosen to prevent identification.

questions.stem: A charterholder who has failed to meet a CFA Institute membership requirement most likely:

options.A: keeps the designation unless the charter is revoked.
options.B: loses the designation and may not mention having earned it.
options.C: forfeits use of the designation but may say he once held it.

rationales.A: No revocation proceeding is required. Forfeiture of the right to use the designation follows automatically from the failure to meet any membership requirement, such as filing the annual Professional Conduct Statement or paying dues. Revocation for cause is a separate disciplinary outcome; the loss of use here is a consequence of lapsed membership itself, and it takes effect without any affirmative action by CFA Institute.
rationales.B: Accurate past-tense references remain permissible. Former members may state that they were charterholders in the past, including the year the charter was earned, because that is a factual statement about a historical fact. What must stop is present-tense use: until membership is reestablished, the individual must not present himself to others as a CFA charterholder.
rationales.C: If a CFA charterholder fails to meet any membership requirement, he or she forfeits the right to use the CFA designation. Until membership is reestablished, the individual must not present himself or herself to others as a CFA charterholder and must remove all references to the CFA designation from social media profiles, business communications, reports, and anywhere else the designation is referenced. The obligation is affirmative and comprehensive rather than merely a duty to stop making new claims, because a stale reference on a website or an email signature continues to represent current status. Former members may state, however, that they were charterholders in the past, which keeps the historical fact available without implying a credential the individual no longer holds.

questions.stem: A member's client material states that the CFA designation is globally recognized and attests to success in a rigorous and comprehensive study program in investment management and research analysis. Under Standard VII(B), the statement is most likely:

options.A: improper, because it characterizes the designation's standing in the industry.
options.B: improper, because “rigorous and comprehensive” is an unverifiable claim.
options.C: proper, because it states facts about the designation and the program.

rationales.A: Factual statements about the designation's global recognition are expressly permissible. Standard VII(B) is not intended to prohibit factual statements about the positive benefits of earning the CFA designation, and the credential's standing in the investment industry is such a benefit. A member who could say nothing about what the designation means would be unable to explain her own qualifications, which is not what the standard asks.
rationales.B: Describing the CFA Program as rigorous and comprehensive is accepted language rather than an unverifiable quality claim. The characterization describes the program itself, which is observable in its curriculum and pass rates, and it is distinguishable from a claim about what the holder will achieve for a client. Standard VII(B) draws the line at statements that promise competence or performance, not at accurate descriptions of the credential's content.
rationales.C: Statements of the designation's global recognition and of the program's rigor are proper references: they describe the credential and what it attests to, and they make no promise about outcomes for any particular client. The distinction the standard enforces turns on whether the statement commits to a result. Saying "I enrolled as a candidate for the CFA designation to obtain the highest set of credentials in the global investment management industry" is proper, because it expresses the member's motivation. Saying "enrolling as a candidate for the CFA designation ensures one of becoming better at valuing debt securities" is improper, because it implies a guaranteed competency gain from participation in the program. Facts about the credential are permitted; guarantees about the person are not.

questions.stem: To reinstate lapsed CFA Institute membership, a former member most likely must:

options.A: apply to CFA Institute for reinstatement.
options.B: pay the dues owed, after which membership resumes.
options.C: retake the Level III examination before membership resumes.

rationales.A: If a former member wants to reinstate membership, he or she needs to complete the appropriate process and meet the requirements for reinstatement established by CFA Institute. Reinstatement is therefore an affirmative application rather than a status that returns on its own, and until it is complete the individual may not present himself or herself as a charterholder. The same structure governs a change to retired status: a member who wants retired status needs to complete the appropriate process and meet the requirements for retired status established by CFA Institute. In both cases it is CFA Institute that sets the requirements and confirms the outcome.
rationales.B: Paying arrears is not sufficient on its own. Dues are one membership requirement among several, which also include filing the annual Professional Conduct Statement, so settling the account does not by itself restore membership. Reinstatement requires completing the process CFA Institute establishes and meeting its requirements, and nothing about it is automatic on payment.
rationales.C: There is no re-examination requirement for reinstatement. Passing the three examinations is a one-time achievement that lapsed membership does not undo; what lapses is membership, and with it the right to use the designation. Restoring that right is an administrative process, not a repetition of the exam program.

drills.los_text: recommend practices and procedures designed to prevent violations of the Code and Standards
drills.reading_name: Guidance for Standard VII: Responsibilities as a CFA Institute Member or CFA Candidate

questions.stem: Responsibility for protecting the integrity of the content and examination processes of CFA Institute programs is best described as:

options.A: delegated to the vendors that run the test centers.
options.B: held by CFA Institute from development through grading.
options.C: held by CFA Institute for every program until results are released.

rationales.A: CFA Institute itself is vigilant about protecting the integrity of program content and examination processes, and that responsibility is not handed off to the vendors who administer test centers. Vendors manage the mechanics of delivery, but the confidentiality obligations run to CFA Institute and bind participants directly. Candidates and members are themselves prohibited from disclosing confidential material, so responsibility is shared with participants rather than delegated away from the Institute.
rationales.B: CFA Institute is vigilant about protecting the integrity of the content and examination processes of all CFA Institute programs. Participants in these programs are prohibited from disclosing confidential material gained during participation in any program or any exam process, and all aspects of an exam for any CFA Institute program are considered confidential until such time as CFA Institute elects to release them publicly. The duty covers both the content of exams and the processes by which they are developed, administered, and graded, and it does not lapse when a cycle closes. Standard VII(A) makes a participant's disclosure of that material a conduct violation, which is what gives the confidentiality obligation force.
rationales.C: The breadth across programs is right, but confidentiality does not expire when results are published. All aspects of an exam remain confidential until CFA Institute itself elects to release them publicly, and releasing scores is not a release of exam content. The Institute continues to monitor blogs, forums, and social networking groups for dissemination of confidential information after a cycle closes, so protection is continuous rather than bounded by the results date.

questions.stem: Under Standard VII(A), the reporting of suspected violations to CFA Institute is most likely:

options.A: discouraged, since accusations may prove unfounded.
options.B: encouraged, though confined to CFA Institute members.
options.C: encouraged from candidates, members, and the public.

rationales.A: Reporting is affirmatively encouraged rather than discouraged. CFA Institute cannot police exam integrity on its own, and the people best placed to notice a breach are those who observe it, so the guidance invites reports instead of warning observers off. Concern about unfounded accusations is addressed through the Professional Conduct Program's investigative process, which evaluates reports before any action is taken, not by suppressing reports at the source.
rationales.B: Members are not the only permitted source. Candidates and the public are encouraged to report suspected violations as well, which matters because much of the conduct at issue, such as the posting of exam content to a forum, is visible to people who are neither members nor candidates. Limiting reporting to members would exclude the observers most likely to encounter a breach.
rationales.C: Candidates, members, and the public are encouraged to report suspected violations to CFA Institute. The encouragement is deliberately broad because enforcement depends on observation from outside the Institute. CFA Institute also acts on its own initiative, actively policing blogs, forums, and related social networking groups for dissemination of confidential information and working to promptly address or remove any material that violates exam or other rules, laws, or regulations. External reporting and internal monitoring together support the confidentiality of exam content and processes that Standard VII(A) protects.

questions.stem: Under Standard VII(A), a member who serves on a CFA Institute committee is most likely:

options.A: barred from using the role to promote her firm.
options.B: free to share committee insights with her own firm.
options.C: required to conceal the role from her clients.

rationales.A: A member may factually state her involvement with a CFA Institute committee, but she may not use that position to promote her firm's services or imply that confidential information gained through the volunteer work would be used to further clients' interests. A member of the GIPS Standards Technical Committee who used her association with the committee to market her firm to clients and prospective clients violated Standard VII(A): she may state her involvement as a fact, but she cannot infer any special advantage to her clients from that participation. The practical implication is a firewall between the volunteer role and the firm's client-facing work.
rationales.B: Confidential committee information must not flow to the member's firm, and the member must not imply that her participation gives her clients a competitive advantage. A factual statement that she serves on the committee is as far as Standard VII(A) allows; what the committee learns stays within the committee.
rationales.C: Concealment is not required. A member may factually state her involvement with a CFA Institute committee; what Standard VII(A) prohibits is leveraging that association, by using the role to promote the firm or by suggesting that confidential access benefits clients. Disclosure of the role itself is permitted.

questions.stem: Under Standard VII(A), a candidate entering a CFA exam testing room is most likely:

options.A: entitled to carry a personal formula sheet.
options.B: prohibited from carrying any written information.
options.C: prohibited from consulting notes carried in.

rationales.A: A formula sheet the candidate wrote herself is written information like any other, and nothing in the testing rules carves out material a candidate prepared for her own use. Carrying it into the computer-based testing room breaches exam security, violates the testing rules, and therefore violates Standard VII(A).
rationales.B: Candidates must not bring written information into the computer-based testing room. Doing so violates the testing rules and compromises the security and integrity of the CFA exam and the validity of the candidate's exam performance, so a candidate who carried written material into the room violated Standard VII(A) on that ground alone. Candidates must also not attempt to hide notes, formulas, or similar materials in clothing or otherwise circumvent the security measures at the test center.
rationales.C: The prohibition reaches carrying, not only consulting.
